title: Show HN: Tanuki – Zero-dependency Active Directory triage operator for Linux
text:
Hi HN,

I built Tanuki (https://github.com/Mafifrizi/tanuki) because I was tired of the dependency hell when auditing Active Directory from Linux jumpboxes or minimal containers.

Most existing Linux AD assessment tooling (like Impacket or BloodHound.py) requires heavy Python virtual environments, dozens of pip packages, and leaves a noisy signature on modern EDRs.

Tanuki takes a protocol-first approach: - Zero external pip dependencies: runs directly using Python standard library ctypes and safe Rust. - Talks directly over raw sockets implementing native ASN.1 DER parsing, Kerberos ticket exchange, and LDAP queries. - Parses modern AD attack surfaces: MS-PAC buffer type 17, Shadow Credentials (msDS-KeyCredentialLink), and Resource-Based Constrained Delegation (RBCD) without external wrappers.

It's MIT licensed. Would love feedback on protocol accuracy or edge cases you've encountered in large enterprise AD environments!

This trail is really what matters in the end, not how you get there.

I treat Lambda purely as compute and ignore everything else related to "serverless". My Lambda's are monolith webapps using Axum Rust framework. Yeah but Nadaraya-Watson kernel smoothing isn't actually 1NN/kNN/weighted kNN.

First of all, the trick relies on imputed 1NN/imputed kNN/imputed weighted kNN. And second of all, you still have to explain how imputed weighted kNN relates to the problem of taking a bunch of x/y pairs and predicting a novel y for some novel x. When you start to unpack all of that it does not look simpler to me than what I wrote.

For the weights, I'm not sure that's as mysterious as you make it seem. The most important thing they learn is, basically syntax. So you have 40k token types to choose from at each prediction, and the vast majority of them are statistically implausible because they are syntactically invalid. At some positions this restriction reduces entropy from ~15-16 bits (or 40k choices) to 2^8 (~200 choices) and in some places it reduces it "only" to 12 or 13 (~8k choices, common when the next token is "approximately a noun").

Once you winnow it down, it's much closer to a moderately big multiple choice problem. And much of that entropy lies just in the model's representation of word co-occurrences.
